entry.content:
London lab Cinelab Film & Digital has built a “Remote Kit” that recreates its digital dailies facility on location, with no servers and no dependence on a local network. The kit is centered on iodyne Pro Data and its Multi-Reader Sharing feature, so ingest, rendering, QC and archiving can run at the same time from one portable unit. According to a new iodyne case study, the kit has gone out on eight productions so far, among them Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine on Easter Island, where the only link to London was satellite internet.

iodyne published this case study on November 10, 2026, you can find it here. We have covered the company several times, from our review of the 48TB Pro Data to the new 96TB and 192TB configurations and the cardless RED RAW ingest cart at Cine Gear 2026. Cinelab came up only last week in our look at the cameras and lenses behind the Camerimage 2026 Golden Frog contenders: the lab processed and scanned the 16mm and Super 8 sequences of Wild Horse Nine. This is iodyne’s own account of the project, so the figures below come from iodyne and Cinelab.

Why dailies now travel with the shoot

Cinelab is a film laboratory, digital dailies and post-production facility in London. It handles everything from dailies and near-set support to deliverables and LTO archiving, and its digital dailies credits include Fantastic Four: First Steps, Deadpool & Wolverine, The Rings of Power, MobLand and The Gentlemen. When a production shoots in or near London, dailies stay in-house. More and more productions, however, shoot far away and ask for the same quality and turnaround on location.

Christy Kail, Cinelab’s Head of Workflow, designs the systems for those jobs. The hard part, he says, is that data volumes change without warning: “You’d have a job calmly shooting 1.5 hours a day, and as soon as they get to a place with nice palm trees, they start shooting six hours a day.”

The case study also quotes film technologist Dane Brehm of Cintegral Technologies. In his view, storage used to sit at the end of a production. Now it sits at the center, and someone on set coordinates ingest, backups, media handoffs and editorial priorities in real time. Brehm calls that role a “data quarterback.”

A server or a stack of drives

Before the Remote Kit, Cinelab had two ways to build a location package. Large multi-unit jobs got a dedicated storage server, with its own portable rack, a soundproofed room and cooling, plus a lot of preparation and setup time. That does not work well in a hotel room or with several moves between locations, and shipping it as air freight was very expensive.

Smaller jobs ran from direct-attached drives, which were hard to scale. Only one machine could mount a drive at a time, so every step waited for the previous one: ingest before renders, renders before QC, QC before archiving. Kail puts it plainly: “Before Pro Data, if you were watching a file, you couldn’t also be rendering it. It didn’t matter how fast your storage was. That didn’t change until multi-reader sharing existed.”

What Multi-Reader Sharing changes

The Remote Kit can go out to any production within 48 hours. At its center is the Pro Data, a Thunderbolt SSD RAID with eight Thunderbolt 3 ports, sustained speeds of up to 5 GB/s, RAID-6 that survives two simultaneous SSD failures, and AES-XTS-256 encryption with keys in a hardware Secure Enclave. Multi-Reader Sharing came with firmware 1.5, and firmware 1.6 brought it to Windows. It lets several computers read the same read-only container at the same time, connected directly over Thunderbolt and without a network.

In Cinelab’s workflow, each ingested batch of media goes into a container that is then locked and shared between the workstations. Every machine reads the original offload, not a copy, so every proxy and archive traces back to the same untouched files. According to the case study, this also builds data discipline into the setup: on a remote set with one or two operators, nobody has to remember which drive holds the original offload.

Downton Abbey: ten cameras and one operator

The proof of concept was Downton Abbey: The Grand Finale (Focus Features and Universal Pictures, produced by Carnival Films, directed by Simon Curtis). For a horse-racing sequence, the production shot on ten cameras, including Sony VENICE 8K and RED V-RAPTOR 8K, and generated 5 to 6TB of data a day. Two to three Mac Studios worked as a render farm off the Pro Data and rendered editorial DNx files directly, with a single Cinelab operator on site. According to iodyne, the job showed that one person could recreate a workflow that normally takes a team.

Wild Horse Nine: 25 days on Rapa Nui over Starlink

Wild Horse Nine shot for 25 days on Easter Island, also called Rapa Nui, with only satellite internet. Cinematographer Ben Davis shot on the ARRI ALEXA 35, with up to three cameras running at once. Cinelab gave each camera its own container on the Pro Data. When a camera’s media had landed, its container was locked and shared as read-only, so offload, rendering, and archiving ran at the same time instead of one after the other.

The operator on the island generated several sets of files and sent them over Starlink to London, where colorist Darren Rae graded them. Cinelab then distributed deliverables to editorial, post, and the studio on several continents. Usable upload speed on the island was sometimes as low as 10 Mbps, so fast file generation left more time for the upload without delaying the overall delivery.

The same kit has since gone to The Agency (Paramount+ with Showtime) in Kenya and Morocco, to MobLand (Paramount+), and to The Buccaneers (Apple TV+) in Central Europe. Each production had a different location and a different infrastructure problem, and each ran on the same portable setup.

About 20 hours of ALEXA 35 footage in RAID-6

Cinelab has now completed eight projects with the Remote Kit, which it sourced through iodyne’s UK distributor, CCK Tech. In RAID-6, the kit holds about 20 hours of ALEXA 35 footage. On a heavy day, that is enough to ingest a full shoot day while the archive of the previous day’s footage finishes, without the two jobs competing for the same drive. The case study does not give the capacity of the standard unit. For multi-unit or very data-heavy productions, Cinelab swaps in a 48TB or 96TB Pro Data.

Kail explains why that flexibility matters: “Because most equipment must be carted and packed several weeks before the shoot begins, it’s not uncommon for the goalposts to move between shipping and shooting. Now we can always have our operator hand-carry an upgraded capacity iodyne to hot-swap into the package, should we find that an extra unit and an array have been booked in the meantime.”

What this means for near-set dailies

The interesting point here is not raw speed. It is that several machines can read the same original camera files at once without a SAN or NAS, so a one-person dailies station can ingest, render and archive in parallel. For DITs and dailies operators who still queue jobs on single drives, that removes the main bottleneck, and the hand-carry upgrade path is a practical answer to schedules that change after the kit has shipped.

As a vendor case study, it also leaves questions open. It names no dailies or transcoding software, gives no price for the kit, and does not say how many copies of the footage stayed on location before the LTO archive. RAID-6 protects against failed SSDs inside the unit, but not against losing the unit itself, so the backup chain on set would be the first thing we would ask about.

Price and availability

The iodyne Pro Data is available in 12TB, 24TB, and 48TB versions, plus the 96TB and 192TB versions that iodyne added in January 2026. The 48TB model lists at $37,995 at B&H. CVP in the UK carries the Pro Data, but gives its price on request only. iodyne’s full case study, with more photos from the sets, is on the iodyne website.

How do you handle dailies on remote shoots: a server, a stack of direct-attached drives, or shared storage like the Pro Data? And how do you get footage home from places with only satellite internet? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: ShotDeck Relaunch Announced – Natural Language Search, Movie and TV Clips, Public Decks
entry.summary: ShotDeck, the cinematic reference library founded by cinematographer Lawrence Sher, ASC, is getting its biggest update since launch. The rebuilt platform combines semantic, natural language search with its human-curated tags, brings 10-second clips to movies and TV, adds camera-m
entry.content:
ShotDeck, the cinematic reference library founded by cinematographer Lawrence Sher, ASC, is getting its biggest update since launch. The rebuilt platform combines semantic, natural language search with its human-curated tags, brings 10-second clips to movies and TV, adds camera-motion filters, a new Discover page, a redesigned Titles section with awards and film-movement filters, and public deck links that work without an account. The relaunch rolls out at ShotDeck.com this month.

We have followed ShotDeck since its early days. We first wrote about it in February 2020, during the free public beta, as a collaborative, searchable library of movie images built by Sher (both Joker films, The Hangover trilogy, Garden State) to solve his own prep problems. A paid subscription followed in 2021, the iOS app arrived in 2024, and today the company says the library holds millions of searchable shots and clips from films, television, music videos and commercials. For a lot of DPs, directors, production designers and agency creatives, it has become the standard place to pull frames for a mood board or a pitch deck.

According to ShotDeck, the team did not reinvent the product but rebuilt the site from the ground up while keeping the core experience intact. Every page and workflow was reworked, and the company describes the result as familiar to existing users, with more ways to search, discover, organize and share references. Sher frames it as a change of mission: “We’re expanding our mission beyond being the most comprehensive, searchable library of cinematic imagery to become the ultimate discovery tool for creative visual inspiration,” he said in the press release.

Natural language search meets human-curated tags

The centerpiece of the relaunch is search. ShotDeck now combines what it calls advanced semantic (vector) search with its existing keywords and technical filters. In practice, this means you can type a full sentence describing a subject, setting, mood, action or visual idea (the press images show queries like “riding horses through the desert” and “a woman in a crowd celebrating at a party”) and then narrow the results with ShotDeck’s filmmaking-specific filters such as color, aspect ratio, optical format, interior or exterior, time of day and number of people.

This is an interesting move in the market. When we covered Flim.ai adding video cuts back in 2023, the main difference between the two platforms was exactly this: Flim relied on AI-based search, while ShotDeck relied on a tag system curated by humans. ShotDeck now offers both, and in my opinion that is the right call. Pure semantic search is fast for rough ideas, but when you need a specific frame size, lighting setup or lens choice, hand-applied technical metadata is still much more reliable (at least for now, but that’s just my guess).

Clips for movies and TV, plus camera-motion filters

ShotDeck Clips existed before, but only for music videos and commercials. With the relaunch, 10-second video clips come to movies and television as well, so you can study a reference in motion instead of as a single still frame. Users can set custom in and out points and export clips as MP4 or GIF files for mood boards, sizzle reels, presentations and educational material. The EPK says clips can be played and exported from “nearly every shot on ShotDeck.”

For anyone who has tried to describe a camera move to a director or a client with a still image, this is probably the most useful addition. It ties in with the new camera-motion filters, which let you search for tracking shots, zooms, pans and tilts. Being able to filter for, say, a slow push-in in a night interior and then hand that clip to your operator or grip team is a real time-saver in prep.

Of course, clips from feature films raise the question of licensing, and the press material does not go into it. ShotDeck positions all of its content as reference, inspiration and education material, so I would treat exported clips as internal prep and pitch material, not as something to cut into a public video.

A Discover page and a redesigned Titles section

The new Discover page now serves as ShotDeck’s home page. It shows trending titles, shots, filmmakers and tags, plus curated collections, and the company says it is meant for open-ended browsing when you don’t yet know exactly what you are looking for.

The Titles page has been redesigned too. You can browse by popularity, alphabetically or by release date (including a poster view), and expanded title pages list cast, crew and top shots. New filters for awards and honors cover the Academy Awards, BAFTAs, Film Independent Spirit Awards and Camerimage, down to specific categories such as Best Cinematography or Costume Design. With Camerimage 2026 having just wrapped, that last filter is a nice way to dig into the cinematography of past winners.

Genres and subgenres have been greatly expanded, from broad categories to niches like Neo-Noir, Cosmic Horror, Cyberpunk and Martial Arts. There are also film movements such as German Expressionism, French New Wave and Black New Wave, as well as Featured Collections built around unexpected connections between titles: Microbudget Masterpieces, First Features, Single Location Films and Actors Who Directed Themselves, among others.

Public decks and workflow upgrades

Decks, ShotDeck’s collections of saved references, can now be shared through a public link that anyone can open without a ShotDeck account. This should make it much easier to send references to clients or crew members who don’t have a subscription. Decks can also be organized into folders, images can be saved quickly to Favorites, a new multi-select tool handles several shots or titles at once, and PDF exports get more advanced formatting options.

Other updates include larger image previews in the shot detail view, improved enterprise account management tools and an expanded ShotDeck Community site with articles, events and offers. Existing tools such as Similar Shots, the Color Picker, the iOS and Android apps and the Canva integration remain. The Canva integration lets you search the library and drag references directly into a Canva project.

ShotDeck also published a short overview video of the platform:

Pricing and availability

The new ShotDeck launches in November 2026 at ShotDeck.com, on the web and in the iOS and Android apps. The press release does not mention any price changes. At the time of writing, ShotDeck’s help center lists an individual plan at $14.95 per month or $119.95 per year (about $9.99 per month), team plans for three to ten users at $12.95 per user per month or $95.40 per user per year, and custom enterprise plans. The company also offers discounts for verified students, educators and institutions. Prices are listed in US dollars only.

I hope ShotDeck keeps growing the clips library at this pace. For now, the combination of semantic search, motion references and account-free sharing looks like a meaningful step for a tool many of us already open at the start of every project.

I just had an amazing conversation about the new ShotDeck with Larry Sher and look forward to sharing that video with the audience next week.

Do you use ShotDeck or a similar reference library in your prep or pitch work? Which of the new features would change your workflow the most? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: rushes Rentals Launched – Vimeo On Demand Alternative with 90% Revenue Share and Rentals from Your Own Website
entry.summary: Today, video-hosting and review platform rushes launches Rentals, a way for filmmakers to rent their films directly to audiences, two days before Vimeo On Demand closes for good on November 20, 2026. Filmmakers set their own prices and territories, keep 90% of each rental after V
entry.content:
Today, video-hosting and review platform rushes launches Rentals, a way for filmmakers to rent their films directly to audiences, two days before Vimeo On Demand closes for good on November 20, 2026. Filmmakers set their own prices and territories, keep 90% of each rental after VAT and payment fees, and can sell from their own website through the standard rushes embed as well as on rushes itself. Let’s take a closer look.

We’ve written about Vimeo quite a bit lately, from how the platform turned away from the filmmakers who built it to 18 years of uploads locked behind a paywall. When rushes launched in March, it focused on hosting, review and portfolio pages. With Rentals, it now also positions itself as a Vimeo On Demand alternative for filmmakers who sell their work directly. According to Vimeo’s shutdown notice, On Demand stopped taking new purchases on September 21, 2026, and all On Demand pages, storefronts and purchase flows go offline on November 20. Viewers also lose access to films they bought or rented there.

Why rushes built Rentals

According to the company, Rentals was not originally on the company’s roadmap. Members of the rushes community asked for it, and the company built it after long conversations with filmmakers who had been selling on Vimeo On Demand. Vimeo pointed those sellers to Vimeo OTT, a separate product built for running a streaming channel, with its own login and pricing. rushes describes that as a much more complex step for an individual filmmaker or a small production company.

A lot of filmmakers were left wondering what they were going to do when Vimeo announced they were pulling VOD. People in our community asked if we could build a replacement, so we did. We kept the design familiar, kept the same 90% deal, and added features they wanted to see.

Guy Loftus, co-founder of rushes and a documentary filmmaker

Rentals deliberately mirrors the way Vimeo On Demand worked, so sellers who move across should find the structure familiar. Each film gets its own page with a trailer, the main film and extras, pricing, and a viewing period, together with the filmmaker’s own poster and wide image.

Part of the existing account, not a second service

Rentals is part of a filmmaker’s rushes account rather than a separate product. A film on sale is built from videos already in the filmmaker’s library and uses the storage their plan already includes, so nothing has to be uploaded twice. The only extra charge is 10% of each rental, with no fixed fee per sale.

The revenue split is the same one Vimeo On Demand offered: the filmmaker keeps 90% of each rental after VAT and payment fees, and rushes takes 10%. rushes acts as the seller, so it charges and pays VAT in the UK and the EU. Filmmakers keep all rights to their films, and only grant rushes the right to distribute them. Payouts are made monthly, within 30 days of the end of the month, once the balance reaches £20, €20 or $20.

For comparison, Vimeo’s OTT pricing breakdown lists a fee of 10% plus 50 cents per transaction for buy-and-rent (TVOD) sales. After the first free hour, OTT upload time is sold in blocks, starting at $99 for up to 10 hours. Vimeo also notes that existing Vimeo account holders can link videos from their Vimeo library to OTT without buying upload hours.

Prices, territories and viewing periods

Filmmakers set their own prices in three currencies: pounds for the UK, euros for the rest of Europe and US dollars for the rest of the world. Viewers see the price with VAT included. Availability can be worldwide, everywhere except named countries, or only in named countries, so a filmmaker can match the territories to the rights they hold. A film can be listed publicly on rushes or be reachable only by link.

The viewing period is also set by the filmmaker. The rental clock starts either at first play, with 30 days to start watching, or at payment. On the live Rentals page at the time of writing, Guy Loftus’s own documentary New Story Run rents for $3.00 with 48 hours to finish once playback starts, while Dirk van den Berg’s The Siege of Mecca allows 72 hours and shows a promotional price.

Renting from your own website

Two features go further than a direct replacement for Vimeo On Demand. The first is the embed. The standard rushes embed code also works for a film on sale: placed on a filmmaker’s own website, the player shows the trailer and a rent button, and viewers can rent the film through the embed without visiting another platform. According to rushes, filmmakers can build a whole website around their rentals this way.

The second is Key dates. Filmmakers can mark the dates when their film is especially relevant, such as an anniversary or an awareness day, and attach the poster, clips, and suggested wording. Around those dates, rushes may feature the film on its Instagram, LinkedIn, and Reddit accounts and in its newsletter. An optional discount can run while the film is promoted.

What do viewers need?

Viewers do not need a subscription. A free rushes account is created at checkout from an email address, and an unused rental can be canceled within 14 days for a refund. Films stream in the browser on a computer, phone, or tablet, and the film pages state that there is no download and that an internet connection is required. The platform’s existing rules also apply to Rentals: no ads, no AI training, and data stored in the EU.

What else has changed at rushes

rushes has also expanded since its launch in March. Paid plans now start with 500GB of storage and can be increased in 500GB blocks, which can be removed again when they are no longer needed. A desktop migrator app can move a Vimeo library while preserving folder structure, descriptions, and privacy settings, and the platform now offers customizable, domain-restricted embeds, along with an API and SDK. According to rushes, an October rebuild made the platform 7.5 times faster.

Current limitations

Only filmmakers on a paid rushes plan can sell films through Rentals. Key dates do not guarantee promotion, as rushes says it may feature a film around the dates supplied by the filmmaker. Rentals are streaming-only for viewers, with no download option. The Vimeo migrator is currently available for Apple silicon Macs, with Intel Mac and Windows versions listed as still to come.

Price and availability

Rentals is available today, November 18, 2026, to filmmakers on a paid rushes plan at rushes.cc/rentals. On the rushes pricing page, the Creator plan is listed at €7.19 per month or €69 per year (£5.99 / £57 at launch), with 500GB of storage included and additional 500GB blocks at €6.00 per month. Beyond the plan, rushes keeps 10% of each rental, with no other fee per sale.

The CineD reader offer from the launch still applies: three months of the Creator plan for free with the code CINED_3_RGL26 at checkout. After that, the plan renews monthly.

Did you sell your films through Vimeo On Demand, and where are you moving them now? Would renting directly from your own website change how you distribute your work? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Aiarty Video Enhancer – Offline AI Denoising, 4K Upscaling and Black Friday Offer
entry.summary: Aiarty has updated its Aiarty Video Enhancer desktop software to version 3.9. The new version lets users pause an export and check the frames that are already processed, and it follows version 3.8, which added recovery of unfinished exports and MKV support. The application runs o
entry.content:
Aiarty has updated its Aiarty Video Enhancer desktop software to version 3.9. The new version lets users pause an export and check the frames that are already processed, and it follows version 3.8, which added recovery of unfinished exports and MKV support. The application runs offline on Windows and Mac and combines AI denoising, deblurring, upscaling to 4K, frame interpolation, audio cleanup, and SDR to HDR conversion in one interface. A Black Friday offer currently reduces the lifetime license by 45%.

We have previously reported on the Aiarty Video Enhancer at its introduction and after an update with new AI models and control options, and we also covered the Aiarty Image Enhancer, which uses a similar approach for still images. Aiarty is a division of Digiarty Software. The company positions the Video Enhancer as a separate enhancement stage that sits next to the editing application, not as a replacement for it: footage is cut in the NLE, and clips that need more resolution, less noise, or smoother motion go through the Video Enhancer before final delivery. As a local video upscaler, Aiarty keeps footage on the user’s computer, helping protect client privacy and avoiding transfer delays. Its lifetime license includes free lifetime updates and commercial use, with no recurring subscription or processing-credit fees, potentially lowering ongoing software costs for frequent users

Three AI models for different footage

The software uses three AI models, and the user selects one per clip. moDetail-HQ v3 is a diffusion and GAN model for fine texture such as hair, skin, foliage, and fabric. Smooth-HQ v3 is a diffusion model for faithful restoration, with gentler deblurring and denoising and a focus on color fidelity. superVideo vHQ, also a diffusion and GAN hybrid, is for very noisy, low-light, and dark interior footage.

moDetail-HQ v3 and Smooth-HQ v3 can upscale by 1x, 2x, or 4x, or to fixed 1K, 2K, and 4K targets. superVideo vHQ works at 2x only. A Strength Control slider sets how strongly each model processes the footage, so users can choose between a subtle, natural result and stronger sharpening. According to Aiarty, the models were trained on 2.38 million images and 120 hours of HD and 4K video.

Denoise, deblur and upscaling

The Denoise Video function targets luminance grain, chroma noise and high ISO artifacts. Aiarty names typical use cases such as concerts in dim venues, indoor scenes and night shots. The same models also handle softness from slight focus errors, compression blocks and pixelation from heavy digital zoom or cropping.

With Upscale Video, sources at 360p, 480p or 540p can be upscaled to HD, 2K or 4K. For productions, this is relevant when cropped shots, archive material, or older camera footage must match 4K material on the same timeline. Because the models are generative, the added detail is reconstructed by the AI and does not come from the source file.

Frame interpolation, audio cleanup and HDR

The frame interpolation module generates new frames to bring footage to 60 or 120fps, or to create 8x and 16x slow motion. Aiarty says that it uses AI-trained flow estimation and motion compensation to avoid warping, smearing, and the jello effect. The company lists live action with fast motion, time-lapse, animation, and 3D renders as suitable material.

An Audio Denoise module removes background noise, clicks, echoes, and wind noise and makes voices clearer, with a real-time preview. A color panel adjusts white balance, exposure, contrast, saturation, highlights and shadows. The experimental HDR function converts SDR 8-bit footage to HDR 10-bit in three modes (Neutral, Bright and Graded), with its own strength slider. Basic edit tools for trimming, cropping, rotating, flipping, and forced deinterlacing complete the feature set.

What is new in versions 3.8 and 3.9

Version 3.9 adds pause and resume for export tasks. When the user pauses an export, the software writes a playable clip of the part that is already processed, and a “View Clip” option opens it. If an export is paused after ten seconds, for example, the clip holds those ten processed seconds. Together with the trim function, this gives a quick way to compare enhancement settings before a full-length export. The update also adds a “Start All Tasks” button to the task queue and support for copying image-based subtitles in MKV files.

Version 3.8 focused on reliability for long clips and batches. Unfinished export tasks can now be recovered and resumed after a restart of the software, instead of starting again from the beginning. Aiarty also optimized CUDA encoding memory management to reduce VRAM usage during demanding exports, added MKV import, improved decoding and export logic for some formats, and added Spanish and Italian interfaces.

Formats, hardware and performance

The Video Enhancer imports a wide range of formats, including MP4, MOV, MXF, MTS, M2TS, MKV, AVI and WebM. Output is MP4, MOV, or MKV with H.264, H.265, ProRes, or AV1. Depending on the codec and profile, the export settings offer YUV 4:2:0, 4:2:2, or 4:4:4.

On Windows 10 or later, the software uses DirectML on AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA GPUs and TensorRT on NVIDIA cards from the GeForce 10 series to the RTX 50 series. Aiarty asks for at least 8GB of RAM (16GB recommended) and 4GB of VRAM on dedicated GPUs (8GB recommended). On macOS 13 or later, it supports Intel Macs with a dedicated GPU and Apple Silicon, with CoreML acceleration.

Turbo Mode prioritizes processing speed. According to Aiarty, upscaling a 25-minute 2K clip at 30fps to 4K takes 25 minutes with Turbo Mode on a Windows PC with an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Step Mode uses tiled AI inference to lower VRAM usage on long, high-resolution clips, at the cost of speed. Batch export processes many clips in one session, and all processing stays on the local computer, with no upload to a cloud service.

Current limitations

The free version processes clips of up to 120 seconds each and adds a watermark; batch export requires a full license. superVideo vHQ, the model for the most difficult low-light footage, is limited to 2x upscaling. The HDR conversion is marked as experimental and needs an HDR-capable display for correct viewing. The speed figures above are Aiarty’s own, and we have not tested them.

Price and availability

Aiarty Video Enhancer is available now for Windows and Mac, and a free trial can be downloaded from the Aiarty website. With the current Black Friday offer, a lifetime license for three Windows PCs or three Macs costs $129 instead of $235, with free lifetime updates. A one-year license for one PC or one Mac costs $79 instead of $99. The Media Enhancer Bundle with the Aiarty Image Enhancer is $199 instead of $390, and the 3-in-1 bundle, which adds Aiarty Image Matting, is $259 instead of $499. All prices are in US dollars, and Aiarty gives a 30-day money-back guarantee.

For more information, please visit the Aiarty website.

Do you use AI enhancement as a separate stage after the edit, or do you keep noise reduction and upscaling inside your NLE? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Panasonic LUMIX SHX1 Interview – Tsumura-san on Blackmagic RAW, Missing ND, S9 Successor, and Firmware Hacks
entry.summary: During my visit to Panasonic’s headquarters in Osaka, I had the chance to sit down with Toshiyuki Tsumura-san, the man in charge of Panasonic’s imaging division. We talked about the new Panasonic LUMIX AU-SHX1 box camera, why it records Blackmagic RAW, why there is no internal ND
entry.content:
During my visit to Panasonic’s headquarters in Osaka, I had the chance to sit down with Toshiyuki Tsumura-san, the man in charge of Panasonic’s imaging division. We talked about the new Panasonic LUMIX AU-SHX1 box camera, why it records Blackmagic RAW, why there is no internal ND filter, and whether Panasonic had to compromise to make filmmakers and broadcasters happy. And of course, I could not leave Osaka without asking about a LUMIX S9 successor, the future of Micro Four Thirds, and the new wave of camera firmware hacks.

For complete coverage of the camera announcement, head to our news article, review, and camera Lab Test. The camera was also added to our camera databases.

NOTE: For the above video, for English translation: please turn SUBTITLES/CAPTIONS “ON”.

Toshiyuki Tsumura-san is Managing Executive Officer in charge of AVC Business, and Director of the Imaging Solution Business Division at Panasonic Corporation. In other words, the LUMIX cameras and Panasonic’s professional video products, from cinema to live production, all report to him. This piece is about the thinking behind the camera, and about a few questions that I know many of you guys have been asking for a while.

The interview was held in Japanese. What you read below is based on the English translation, and I shortened some of the answers so they are easier to read. If you want to hear every word, the full interview is in the video above. So, sit back and make yourself comfortable.

A new kind of multi-purpose camera

CineD: What are the core advantages of the new camera?

Tsumura-san: For us, this is a camera with a new concept. One body covers everything from entry-level video production to full-scale cinema shooting and live streaming. It combines the technology we refined in LUMIX with the technology we refined in our professional AV business. Phase-detection autofocus and image stabilization are packed into an expandable box-style body with a vari-angle monitor, which no camera of ours had before. Add a grip, and you shoot with the freedom of a mirrorless camera, for YouTube content or lightweight cinema.

For cinema, we added Blackmagic RAW recording in addition to ProRes RAW, and for the first time, we worked with ARRI so that ARRI LogC3 comes pre-installed. On a set where ARRI cameras are the A-cameras, our camera can work as the B-camera, and in some cases, it can shoot entire scenes with the ARRI look. We also kept Open-Gate, so the camera is ready for vertical video. For live streaming, it keeps our full-frame LUMIX image quality, and our professional AV engineers added the input and output interfaces that live production needs, plus support for multi-camera setups and remote camera systems. We were also very particular about low latency, both when you pull focus and in live production.

Two years since the integration

CineD: How long does it take to develop such a camera, and how do you make sure that you build cameras for the future and not for the past?

Tsumura-san: That is a difficult question. We could only build this concept because our professional AV business and our LUMIX business were integrated two years ago, in 2024. That let us hear directly from professionals in live production and on film sets, not only from consumer creators. We listened to more than 100 creators in total, and that is roughly how long it took to go from concept to product. In the end, we went far enough that the camera can be built into our own KAIROS switcher systems for live production.

“We have not compromised at all”

CineD: Panasonic has made box cameras before, but this one has to satisfy filmmakers and broadcasters. Did you have to compromise so that both groups are happy?

Tsumura-san: We have not compromised at all. We focused on the needs both sides share, and the box made the camera more attractive, not less. The box form gives mobility and expandability at the same time. With in-body image stabilization and a vari-angle monitor, the box plus a grip gets close to the mobility of a mirrorless camera. For professional use, we also designed it for heat dissipation and stability when the camera runs for long periods. From a professional point of view, the box style is the best form factor, and the feedback from more than 100 creators made that possible.

Blackmagic RAW, and will it ever go internal?

CineD: Will internal Blackmagic RAW recording be possible in the future?

Tsumura-san: Recording Blackmagic RAW on a camera that is not a Blackmagic camera is a first for the industry, and we are proud that we finished it in close cooperation with Blackmagic. Recording Blackmagic RAW directly to an SSD is also new. Proxy recording, on the other hand, goes to the internal CFexpress Type B card, which should make the editing workflow more efficient. We have received many requests to record Blackmagic RAW internally rather than to an external SSD; we are very aware of that need, and we continue to work on it for future development.

Why there is no internal ND filter

CineD: The camera looks large enough to hold an internal ND filter. Did you consider one, and if yes, why is it not here?

Tsumura-san: Whether to include a built-in ND filter was a point we struggled with a lot. We wanted many functions in a compact body, and combining a built-in ND with in-body image stabilization was very difficult, so we had to choose one. When we interviewed our creators, they told us strongly that LUMIX image stabilization is essential on set, so we gave it priority. We also know how important an electronic ND is, so we took a new approach with a third-party partner, Tilta. Their external variable ND, announced at the same time, works from the same controls on the camera body, so you change the ND the way you change shutter speed or iris. With this collaboration, we answer both wishes: the ND and the stabilization.

A new line, not a VARICAM or EVA successor

CineD: Looking at the camera name, I see that you carry on the VARICAM and EVA heritage. Should we see this as the first camera in a completely new line?

Tsumura-san: Thank you, that is a good question. This product is a new concept and not a simple successor to earlier models such as the VARICAM or the EVA. It takes the thinking and know-how from both earlier series and combines them with the mobility and image quality of the LUMIX series. Please see it as our first step in a new initiative.

What is different from the LUMIX S1II?

CineD: In components and recording capabilities, the new camera is very similar to the LUMIX S1II. Can you please highlight the differences?

Tsumura-san: On a spec sheet, the recording performance looks similar, but this is not simply that camera in a box. The main difference is the concept: it is a step-up camera for professional and semi-professional creators who want to take on work one level higher, and it is built as a serious cinema camera in image quality, reliability, connectivity, and expandability.

The image sensor is new. The resolution looks the same as the S1II at 24 megapixels, but this time we added an optical low-pass filter, and we tuned the noise reduction for V-Log and ARRI LogC3 to keep very fine detail while suppressing moiré. That know-how combines the best parts of the VARICAM and the LUMIX S1H. Blackmagic RAW was not in the S1II, and the open gate mode is improved. 12G-SDI output, timecode input, and V-mount battery support are what professional sets ask for, and low-latency output for live work and focus pulling also sets it apart. Heat is important too: the S1II had a recording time limit, while this camera has a proper heat-dissipation structure and records without a limit, including at 4K 120p. And for the first time for us, it supports 32-bit float recording from the microphone input, so the body alone gives you audio that does not clip.

Three reasons to choose LUMIX

CineD: The price of the SHX1 puts it in Sony FX5 territory. Can you highlight three reasons why people should consider LUMIX over the competition?

Tsumura-san: The concept is quite different, but I would pick three points. First, flexible workflows: V-Log, ARRI LogC3, ProRes RAW recording, and Blackmagic RAW recording, so creators can choose what fits their environment. Second, despite the compact body, the camera records without a limit at 4K 120p, and it has in-body stabilization, a vari-angle monitor and excellent autofocus, so it is as comfortable as a mirrorless camera and reliable enough for professional sets and run-and-gun work. Third, live production: it supports interfaces and protocols that drop straight into KAIROS systems, plus 12G-SDI and expandable multi-camera and remote operation, so it can be used in real professional live-streaming environments.

A trigger to step up

CineD: Is there anything else you would like to say about the new camera?

Tsumura-san: Our main purpose was not only high specs. Many creators are limited by their equipment or their shooting environment, and they want to make better work or try a new kind of project. We want to give those people a way to step up. We also want to stay with them after they buy the camera, through services, support, and third-party options, so they succeed in those challenges.

Is Panasonic’s footprint big enough?

CineD: Panasonic has brought innovative solutions to filmmakers for many years, yet its footprint is not as big as I would love it to be. Why do you think that is, and how do you want more people to use your very capable cameras?

Tsumura-san: Thank you for the comment. We do not really look at the whole mirrorless market at a macro level. Seen that way, our share can look low. But as a challenger, we focus on clear customer groups: creators who enjoy both video and stills and make hybrid content, customers who carry a small, light camera every day, and customers like those for this camera, who want to make serious cinema work. Measured by the number of people who connect with the LUMIX concept and keep using their cameras, LUMIX fans have increased year by year. So rather than focusing on macro-level market share, we want to keep creating together with our customers and grow together with them.

A LUMIX S9 successor with an EVF?

CineD: The LUMIX S9 (and L10) is well received by the community, and you got a lot of feedback from users. Can we expect a successor soon, maybe with a built-in EVF?

Tsumura-san: The LUMIX S9 has no viewfinder because we designed it for people stepping up from smartphones, who shoot on the monitor like on a phone. Many people support that approach, and it has been a popular model. Still, many customers tell us they want a viewfinder for serious photo and video work. More than two years have passed since the release; we have heard that voice strongly, and technology has moved on. We are working hard to meet your expectations. That is all I can say today.

What about Micro Four Thirds?

CineD: The LUMIX GH7 came out more than two years ago. Is a new Micro Four Thirds flagship camera in the making?

Tsumura-san: The GH7 was developed to be very complete, including ARRI LogC3 support, and many fans still use it. New customers keep buying it today. Micro Four Thirds has a clear appeal that is different from our full-frame L-Mount series: small, light bodies and lenses, and a wide range of lenses that are already available. For video, it also gives you unlimited recording and smaller telephoto lenses. Our position has not changed: this is a very important system for us. For today, I would prefer not to comment on any potential successor models. But offering distinctive products in both Micro Four Thirds and full frame is one of our strengths, so please look forward to it.

AI and firmware hacks

CineD: AI is changing a lot, and many independent programmers are vibe coding new camera firmware that lets people do more with the same hardware. I do not expect Panasonic to support this publicly, but what is your opinion about it, and can Panasonic take advantage of this trend?

Tsumura-san: AI will be very important for cameras as it evolves. But we think the right way is to build AI in-house, to support our customers’ workflows and improve image quality, and then offer it to creators. We understand customers who hack their cameras and rewrite the firmware themselves, and it is probably difficult to stop that trend. But it is very risky for reliability, safety, and security, so we cannot recommend it. We want our customers to actively share their feedback on what they would like to see improved. It is then our responsibility to respond to those needs and continue evolving the camera through firmware updates. That relationship with our customers is the most important thing for us.

Thank you, Osaka

I would like to thank Tsumura-san for his time and for his very open answers, Kanda Kaito-san, and the Panasonic team in Osaka for hosting me. For full camera coverage, please read our LUMIX SHX1 news article, review, and Lab Test.

Guys, what do you think about the LUMIX SHX1 concept, and would you trade a built-in ND for in-body stabilization? Please share your thoughts with us in the comment section below!

entry.title: Panasonic LUMIX AU-SHX1 Announced – 6K Full-Frame Box Camera, OLPF, Blackmagic RAW Recording to SSD, ARRI LogC3 Pre-installed
entry.summary: Panasonic has announced the LUMIX AU-SHX1, a compact box-style cinema camera that brings its LUMIX and professional AV lines together in one body. The Panasonic LUMIX SHX1 is built around a 6K full-frame 24.1MP partially stacked CMOS sensor with an optical low-pass filter, and Pa
entry.content:
Panasonic has announced the LUMIX AU-SHX1, a compact box-style cinema camera that brings its LUMIX and professional AV lines together in one body. The Panasonic LUMIX SHX1 is built around a 6K full-frame 24.1MP partially stacked CMOS sensor with an optical low-pass filter, and Panasonic rates it at up to 15 stops of dynamic range in V-Log. This is the first LUMIX camera to record Blackmagic RAW to an external SSD and to ship with ARRI LogC3 pre-installed. The camera also offers internal ProRes RAW, 12G-SDI, timecode, unlimited 4K 120p recording, phase-detection autofocus, in-body stabilization, and a top-mounted monitor.

For complete coverage of the camera announcement, head to our review, our interview with Panasonic’s head of the imaging division, Tsumura-san, and our camera Lab Test. The camera was also added to our camera databases.

Panasonic merged its professional AV and consumer imaging businesses in 2024, and the SHX1 is the first camera that combines both. Panasonic describes it as its entry into the cinema camera market, positioned between the LUMIX hybrid cameras on one side and its PTZ and live production systems on the other. Compact cinema cameras were already a topic when we spoke with Panasonic’s Toshiyuki Tsumura-san at CP+ 2026, but now, we have conducted a fresh interview with him, talking about the new camera and what the future might bring to Panasonic. According to Panasonic, the main target group is small crews of five people or fewer, often with one person operating the camera, who want to move on to larger and higher-budget productions. The company also sees the SHX1 as a compact B-camera on bigger sets.

A 6K full-frame sensor with an optical low-pass filter

The SHX1 uses a 6K full-frame partially stacked CMOS sensor with 24.1MP effective for video. Panasonic places high-speed processing circuitry above and below the pixel area, and says this reduces rolling shutter distortion and supports high frame rates and fast autofocus. An optical low-pass filter in front of the sensor should suppress moiré and false color on fine patterns. A new engine with a newly developed image processing pipeline handles the high-bitrate data from the sensor, and according to Panasonic, it also reduces latency on the external video outputs.

Panasonic’s Dual Native ISO switches between a low ISO and a high ISO circuit in each pixel, with Auto, Low, and High settings. The ISO range is 100 to 51,200, expandable to 50 to 204,800. Dynamic Range Boost combines both circuits per pixel, weighting a saturation-priority signal from the low ISO circuit and a low-noise signal from the high ISO circuit by the amount of light each pixel receives. Panasonic specifies 15 stops of V-Log/V-Gamut recording with Dynamic Range Boost on and more than 14 stops with it off. Keep your eyes out for our independent LUMIX SHX1 camera Lab Test. The company also notes that with Dynamic Range Boost active, ISO settings is restricted, and rolling shutter distortion increases.

For noise processing, Panasonic says the SHX1 keeps fine detail and natural texture rather than removing all noise, a philosophy it carries over from the VARICAM and the LUMIX S1H. For direct delivery, the camera offers LUMIX Photo Styles, including the Cinelike A2, Cinelike D2 and Cinelike V2 profiles.

Blackmagic RAW, ProRes RAW and ARRI LogC3 in one body

Panasonic sums up the SHX1’s recording options as “3 cinema cameras in 1 body.” The first is Blackmagic RAW, which the camera records directly to an external SSD over USB-C (10Gbps). These are the Blackmagic RAW SSD modes Panasonic lists:

  • 6K 3:2 open gate (5952 x 3968) at 24.00p and 23.98p, with a slight crop
  • 5.8K 17:9 (5760 x 3040) up to 29.97p
  • 5.3K 3:2 (5376 x 3584) at 29.97p and 25.00p
  • 4.4K 3:2 (4416 x 2944) up to 48.00p
  • 3.8K 3:2 (3840 x 2560) up to 59.94p
  • C4K 17:9 (4096 x 2160) up to 59.94p

Recording settings include constant bitrate at 3:1, 5:1, 8:1, and 12:1 and constant quality at Q0 and Q5. Panasonic gives an example of the storage savings: 6K 24p Blackmagic RAW at 12:1 runs at 599Mbps and fits about 445 minutes on a 2TB SSD, while 5.8K 29.97p ProRes RAW at 2,799Mbps fits about 95 minutes on the same drive. For monitoring and grading, users can choose between V-Log and Blackmagic Generation 5 Color Science, which should make it easier to mix the SHX1 with Blackmagic cameras on a multi-camera shoot. Over HDMI to a Blackmagic Video Assist, the SHX1 outputs RAW for Blackmagic RAW recording in 6K 3:2 (6000 x 4000) and 5.9K 16:9 up to 29.97p, 5.7K 17:9 up to 59.94p, and C4K up to 119.88p.

ProRes RAW is the second route. The SHX1 records ProRes RAW HQ and ProRes RAW internally to a CFexpress Type B card in 5.8K 17:9 up to 29.97p and in C4K up to 59.94p. Panasonic’s overview also lists ProRes RAW recording to an SSD. RAW output over HDMI for ProRes RAW on an external recorder covers 6K 3:2 and 5.9K 16:9 up to 29.97p, 5.7K 17:9 up to 59.94p, and C4K up to 119.88p. The camera also records ProRes, H.264 and H.265 in MOV, and H.264 and H.265 in MP4, with proxy recording available.

The third is ARRI LogC3 with ARRI Wide Gamut 3, which comes pre-installed on a LUMIX camera for the first time. It is available for 10-bit recording in video mode. Panasonic highlights the use of ARRI Looks and productions that combine the SHX1 with ARRI digital cinema cameras, and points out that the ALEXA 35 uses LogC4 instead. V-Log and V-Gamut remain available, with the same gamma and color characteristics as the rest of the LUMIX S and G series.

Open gate, high frame rates and vertical anamorphic

Panasonic says the fast readout of the sensor lets the SHX1 record open gate (3:2) in 6K up to 30p and 5.1K up to 60p in 4:2:0 10-bit, plus Blackmagic RAW 6K 24p. A new 3.8K open gate mode records up to 48p in 4:2:2 10-bit. Panasonic positions open gate as a way to deliver several aspect ratios, such as 16:9 and 9:16, from one take.

Beyond open gate, the camera records 6K 2.4:1, 5.9K 16:9 and 5.8K 17:9 up to 60p in 4:2:0 10-bit. C4K, 4K and Cs4K (2.4:1) are available up to 120p in 4:2:0 10-bit and up to 60p in 4:2:2 10-bit, and Full HD goes up to 240p in 4:2:2 10-bit. Some high frame rate modes crop the image: Panasonic lists approximately 1.17x for C4K at 120p and 100p, 1.24x for 4K at 120p and 100p, and 1.21x for Full HD at 240p.

For vertical content shot with anamorphic lenses, the SHX1 adds Vertiscope, a vertical de-squeeze display with 2.0x, 1.6x and 1.33x factors. The de-squeezed image is also available on the HDMI and SDI outputs, so an external monitor shows the correct vertical frame. Panasonic says the box design is made to work in landscape as well as portrait orientation.

Phase-detection AF and in-body stabilization

Autofocus is handled by Phase Hybrid AF with 779 points. Panasonic says AI-based eye and face detection keeps focus even when a face is tilted or partially covered, and Tracking AF should stay on the intended subject when several people cross the frame. Real-time Recognition AF covers people, animals, cars, motorcycles, bicycles, airplanes, and trains.

The SHX1 also has a 5-axis in-body image stabilizer, and Dual I.S. 2 combines it with 2-axis optical stabilization in compatible lenses. For walking shots, Active I.S. adapts the correction for pitch, yaw, and roll, and Advanced E.I.S. reduces perspective distortion. Boost I.S. holds a static handheld composition, Cropless Mode reduces distortion at wide angles without changing the angle of view, and stabilization also works with anamorphic lenses, including roll compensation.

Body, monitor and connections

The SHX1 is an L-Mount camera that measures 110.7 x 112.6 x 120.2mm (4.36 x 4.43 x 4.73in) and weighs about 984g (2.17lb), body only. A metal exterior spreads heat evenly, and a large cooling fan moves it out of the body. According to Panasonic, this allows unlimited recording up to 4K 120p within the guaranteed operating temperature range.

Panasonic calls the monitor the first top-mounted monitor on a LUMIX camera. It tilts up or swings out to the side and stays visible with the top handle attached. The control layout follows LUMIX conventions, with dedicated WB, ISO, and IRIS buttons and an AF ON button. Tally lamps on the front and rear are visible from four directions and can be switched on or off independently.

Power comes from a micro V-mount battery, which can also supply connected accessories. A dedicated USB-C power input accepts a USB PD AC adapter for longer sessions, which requires an adapter and cable rated at 100W (20V/5A). A second USB-C port (10Gbps) connects the SSD, and Panasonic plans to let it charge a smartphone running LUMIX Flow via USB PD with a firmware update in the first half of 2027. Two more terminals are reserved for optional accessories.

For monitoring, the SHX1 has 12G-SDI, which outputs up to 4K 60p over a locking BNC connector, and HDMI. Both outputs work at the same time, for example, to record externally over HDMI while a monitor receives the SDI feed. A TC IN/OUT BNC terminal syncs timecode with a generator or other cameras, and Bluetooth timecode generators are supported as well. On the audio side, the SHX1 is the first LUMIX camera to record 32-bit float audio internally through the 3.5mm microphone input, without an XLR adapter.

Grip, XLR handle and live production unit

Panasonic has three accessories for the SHX1. The AU-GRP1 control grip has dedicated WB, ISO, and IRIS buttons, a joystick, an Fn button, and a zoom rocker, and attaches to the camera via an ARRI-standard rosette. It controls the camera over a wired connection, so it also works on tripods and shoulder rigs. The zoom rocker is designed for a power zoom lens for the SHX1 that Panasonic is currently developing, and with other LUMIX lenses, it operates the crop zoom.

The AU-XHU1 XLR handle unit adds two XLR inputs with 32-bit float recording and high-resolution audio at 96kHz/24-bit. Combined with the camera’s 3.5mm microphone input, it enables 4-channel audio. The handle has a cold shoe, threaded mounting points, and a REC button, and the XLR unit and the top handle can be separated.

The AU-LPU1 Live Production Unit is scheduled for the first half of 2027. It adds Genlock IN, a PoE++ LAN terminal for power, camera control, and IP video over a single cable, and support for a common IP control protocol used by Panasonic’s PTZ camera systems. Panasonic shows the SHX1 with the AU-LPU1 on a remote pan/tilt head, controlled from its studio and PTZ remote panels and the Media Production Suite software, and as a point-of-view camera for esports, indoor sports and music venues. Its system diagram currently shows this setup with the AW-UB50 box camera.

Panasonic also worked with Tilta. Connected over USB-C, the Tilta Nucleus 2.4G Wireless Control Hub (Panasonic) lets the SHX1 control a Tilta Mirage variable ND with the same interface the camera uses for shutter speed, iris and ISO. With a Tilta controller, focus on L-Mount lenses can be pulled without a lens motor.

LUMIX Flow 1.8.0 and LUMIX Lab 3.2.0

Panasonic’s smartphone apps get SHX1 support on December 22, 2026. LUMIX Flow 1.8.0 adds two functions for the SHX1 only. Smartphone Sync Recording stores a simplified copy of each take on the phone, so clips can be played back and rated without a connection to the camera. Sequential Play plays the takes marked as OK in storyboard order, which gives a quick view of the complete sequence on set without an editing application.

LUMIX Flow 1.8.0 also introduces Frame Preview, which crops the live view to a selected frame when the phone switches between vertical and horizontal orientation. This is intended for open gate shoots that deliver 16:9 and 9:16 at the same time, and the cropped view also works on mirrored and external monitors. LUMIX Lab 3.2.0 adds SHX1 support, and both apps add support for iOS 27 and Android 17.

Price and availability

The Panasonic LUMIX SHX1 costs $4,697.99 / €5,199 for the body only. The AU-SHX1U kit, which adds the AU-GRP1 control grip and the AU-XHU1 XLR handle unit, costs $5,497.99 / €5,999. The AU-XHU1 XLR handle unit costs $597.99, and the AU-GRP1 control grip costs $447. The euro prices include VAT. Panasonic plans to ship the camera from the factory in December 2026, so most customers should receive it in January 2027.

The AU-LPU1 Live Production Unit follows in the first half of 2027, and the power zoom lens is still in development. The LUMIX Flow and LUMIX Lab updates are scheduled for December 22, 2026.

Would Blackmagic RAW to an SSD and pre-installed ARRI LogC3 make the LUMIX SHX1 your A-camera on small-crew jobs, or would it work as a B-camera on your bigger sets? And does a box camera with in-body stabilization and phase-detection AF change the way you rig for handheld work? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Nikon ZR Firmware 2.00 Reportedly Coming November 24 – High ISO NR for ProRes N-Log, Full HD Limit for LUT Over HDMI
entry.summary: Nikon has published a dedicated page for firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, and it adds details that were not in the November 3 press release. The selectable High ISO NR also works in ProRes 422 HQ with N-Log, and a 3D LUT on the HDMI output limits that output to Full HD. Ni
entry.content:
Nikon has published a dedicated page for firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, and it adds details that were not in the November 3 press release. The selectable High ISO NR also works in ProRes 422 HQ with N-Log, and a 3D LUT on the HDMI output limits that output to Full HD. Nikon still marks the download as coming soon, but a release on November 24 has been reported. Nikon has not confirmed that date.

We covered the full feature list when Nikon announced firmware 2.00 for the Nikon ZR: Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB for H.265 recording, a selectable High ISO NR level, more assignable controls, focus peaking in R3D NE with a LUT applied, 3D LUT output over HDMI and reduced black-level flicker in dark scenes. The new ZR firmware 2.00 page from Nikon Europe and a short Nikon Europe video now fill in some of the gaps. If you missed it, our Nikon ZR review shows how the camera handles on set.

High ISO NR also for ProRes 422 HQ

In the press release, Nikon described four [High ISO NR] levels for H.265 recording with Log3G10 or N-Log. The firmware page names the four levels (Off, Low, Normal and High) and lists three recording combinations: H.265 with Log3G10, H.265 with N-Log, and ProRes 422 HQ with N-Log. R3D NE is not on the list.

The custom controls are also more specific now. ISO sensitivity, exposure compensation, white balance and color temperature can be assigned to the command dials, and an Fn button can switch the monitor view between the selected LUT and the flat log image.

Limits of the LUT on the HDMI output

A footnote on the page lists the limits of the new 3D LUT on the HDMI output. With a LUT applied, the HDMI output is limited to Full HD. At 60p or 50p, the output frame rate stays at 60p or 50p, but Nikon says the image refresh rate is halved. Depending on the video settings, the HDMI connection can also drop out; according to Nikon, this does not happen when the LUT is applied to the rear monitor.

For operators who need a full-resolution feed, a clean log signal over HDMI with the LUT loaded on the external monitor, or the Log3G10 LUTs of their choice, stays an option. Nikon also notes that [View Assist] can be switched during recording, but the 3D LUT itself cannot be turned on or off while the camera records.

Price and availability

According to reports, firmware 2.00 will be available for download from November 24, Japan time (the evening of November 23 in the US). Nikon has not confirmed this date. The firmware page shows “Free download coming soon”, and the Nikon Download Center lists version 1.11 from March 17, 2026, as the current ZR firmware. In its press release, Nikon says firmware 2.00 is scheduled to be available before the end of the year, as a free update. The Nikon ZR body is available for $2,196.95 at B&H and for €1,998.39 / £1,999 at CVP.

Does the Full HD limit change how you plan to monitor with the Nikon ZR, or will you keep the LUT on your external monitor? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Camerimage 2026 Winners – Golden Frog for Łukasz Żal and Fatherland, Shot in Black and White on ARRI ALEXA 35
entry.summary: Łukasz Żal has won the Golden Frog at Camerimage 2026 for Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, a black-and-white film shot on the ARRI ALEXA 35. The Silver Frog went to Jasper J. Spanning for Woman Unknown, and the Bronze Frog to Mikhail Krichman for Minotaur. Two of the three top fil
entry.content:
Łukasz Żal has won the Golden Frog at Camerimage 2026 for Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, a black-and-white film shot on the ARRI ALEXA 35. The Silver Frog went to Jasper J. Spanning for Woman Unknown, and the Bronze Frog to Mikhail Krichman for Minotaur. Two of the three top films were shot on ARRI cameras, and one on the Sony VENICE 2.

The festival announced the winners at its Closing Gala in Toruń, Poland, on November 14, at the end of the 34th edition, which now runs under the name ToruńCAMERIMAGE. The official list of laureates covers all competitions, from features and documentaries to music videos and student films. A jury led by film editor Joe Walker chose the main competition winners. Before the gala, we looked at the cameras and lenses behind all 15 Golden Frog contenders, and all three winners come from that list.

Golden Frog: Fatherland on the ALEXA 35

Żal shot Fatherland on the ARRI ALEXA 35, according to ARRI’s summary of the Cannes 2026 selection. The film is in black and white, and Pawlikowski has said that most scenes were lit with a single source. The lenses are not public. Żal and Pawlikowski worked together before on Ida and Cold War, which are also black-and-white films.

Silver and Bronze Frogs

Jasper J. Spanning shot May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown on the ARRI ALEXA Mini LF. IndieWire’s Venice camera survey lists vintage Olympus Zuiko lenses and Petzval lenses rehoused by TLS for the production.

Mikhail Krichman shot Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur on the Sony VENICE 2 in 8K X-OCN XT with Cooke anamorphic lenses. The production also tested the ALEXA 35 and selected the VENICE 2 for its flexibility in dark scenes, as DIT Veronica Tiron explains in an interview with the French DIT association ADIT. Minotaur is the only production in the top three that did not use an ARRI camera.

Winners of the other competitions

The festival gave Golden Frogs and Tadpoles in these categories:

  • Cinematographers’ Debuts: Eira Wyn Jones for Effi o Blaenau, directed by Marc Evans
  • Directors’ Debuts: Kaifeng Zhong for Atlantic Rhapsody
  • Documentary Features: Eva Kraljević for To Hold a Mountain, directed by Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić
  • Documentary Shorts: Maxim Arbugaev and Vladimir Egorov for Chuuraa, directed by Evgenia Arbugaev
  • Music Videos: cinematographer Jeff Bierman and director (LA)HORDE for “What You Want” by Angèle ft. Justice; special mention for director Romain Gavras for “Storm” by GENER8ION
  • TV Series: Maciej Sobieraj for Silent Night, directed by Jan Holoubek
  • Polish Feature Films: Alan Ruczyński for A Free Woman, directed by Eliza Godlewska and Alan Ruczyński
  • Student Etudes (Laszlo Kovacs Student Award): Golden Tadpole to Francesca Avanzini for Revolver, Silver Tadpole to Paul Ader for Nika’s Room, Bronze Tadpole to Enrico Barbaro Jr. for Until We Bury Them!

During the festival week, Janusz Kamiński received the THR Visionary in Cinematography award, Darren Aronofsky the award for director, Joe Walker the award for film editor, and Hype Williams the award for achievements in music video. Earlier in the week, Thomas Riedel received the European Film Industry Preservation Award, as we reported.

FilmLight Colour Awards 2026

The sixth FilmLight Colour Awards were presented at the festival on November 8. The awards are for colorists, and they accept work graded on any platform. Greg Fisher of Company 3 won the Theatrical Feature category for Bugonia, his second win in this category after Poor Things. Aidan Farrell of The Farm Post Production won TV Series / Episodic for Lord of the Flies, and Andu Radu of Abator won Spotlight & Documentary for The President’s Cake.

In the Commercial category, Nadia Khairat Gómez won for The North Face’s “Defy Easy.” Imri Agmon of S EC Studio won Emerging Talent for KidSuper’s fashion film “The Boy Who Jumped the Moon.” Two Golden Frog contenders were also on the Theatrical Feature shortlist: Growth of the Soil, graded by Didrik Bråthen (TMLS), and Project Hail Mary, graded by David Cole (FotoKem).

Did the jury choose the right film for the Golden Frog, and which of the winning films do you want to see first? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!
